title: The King James Bible (1611)
hookLine: scholars working in companies produce an English Bible whose phrases are still in the language
carry: the language of heaven, in english

cards: The salt of the earth. A law unto themselves. The powers that be.
Fight the good fight. The skin of my teeth. People say these without a second thought, at work, in sports commentary, in arguments about politics.
Every one sits, word for word, in the same old book. In the book of Job, a man who has lost nearly everything says: "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth."
The book is an English Bible made at the order of a king, and its sound has hung around in the language ever since.

teach.h: A NEW TRANSLATION, ORDERED BY A KING.
teach.b: King James ruled England and Scotland when English Christians were reading more than one translation, and arguing about them. So a new one was ordered, to be read aloud in churches.
Teams of scholars took different parts of the Bible, and their versions were checked and revised together.
The title page says it was translated out of the original tongues, with the former translations diligently compared and revised. That last part matters. The translators didn't start from nothing.
They leaned on English Bibles that came before, including the work of William Tyndale, who had been executed as a heretic.

teach.h: A WINDOW TO LET IN THE LIGHT.
teach.b: Their preface to the reader uses a string of pictures for what translation does: it opens a window to let in the light, it breaks the shell so we can eat the kernel, it pulls back the curtain.
And the result was made for the ear. Listen to the twenty-third Psalm: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters."
Short words, a steady beat, made to be said out loud in a stone church. Some Christians still read the King James as their main Bible, and others treasure it alongside newer translations.
Either way, its rhythm is why today's line fits: the language of heaven, in english.

how: Some churches read the King James Version in every service, while others use newer translations and keep the King James for familiar passages such as Psalm 23, read at funerals.

practice: Read Psalm twenty-three aloud, from a Bible or a phone if you have one, or just the lines from today: the LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

Read slowly, at a speaking volume, as if to a room, then sit with the sound still in the air. If you pray, let the psalm become your prayer; if you don't, notice the rhythm and what it does to your breath.
